newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA TO SELL 30 PCT OF KREMIKOVTZI STEEL PLANT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA TO SELL 30 PCT OF KREMIKOVTZI STEEL PLANT.

text.p: Bulgaria has drawn up a programme to privatise and restructure the vast Kremikovtzi steelworks, selling off smaller units and offering a 30 percent capital stake to investors.

A shareholders meeting on August 6 will vote on a restructuring plan drawn up with the government allowing for the sale of some 60 small workshops around the plant and eight medium-sized units as independent businesses.
The draft also foresees the sale of a 30 percent stake in the plant by the end of the year.
Executive Director Dimitar Milushev said South Korea's Samsung Corp, Japan's Mitsubishi Corp and some Russian firms had shown potential interest in the plant, Bulgaria's biggest steelworks.

The plant's management changed in February after the former Socialist government stepped down. "In the last four months we have increased output by 30 percent and sales by 33 percent," said Milushev, adding that they had cut gas and electricity costs and shed 500 jobs from a workforce of 17,000.
Kremikovtzi, the size of a small town, dominates the plain below the Balkan Range mountains 25 km (15 miles) northeast of Sofia with huge chimneys belching thick white and orange smoke.
It has its own bus service and 492 km (305 miles) of rail track, and consumes 35,000 cubic metres of gas an hour.
Parts of the plant, which opened in 1964, have been modernised, while some older ones lie derelict.
Kremikovtzi is 96 percent state-owned, with the other four percent held by employees or former employees through Bulgaria's mass voucher privatisation scheme.

Milushev put annual sales turnover at $550 million and said the plant had repaid debts of $24.5 million since February. He said outstanding debts totalled $10 million to banks and $7 million to suppliers.
He said improvements in cash flow had allowed the plant to let local clients defer payments, boosting sales within Bulgaria by 150 percent. He planned to cut the workforce to 15,900 by year end.
"My dream is to sell 50 percent of production in Bulgaria by the end of the year," Milushev said.

Kremikovtzi has a sales quota of 450,000 tonnes to the European Union, and also exports further afield. It has a barter deal with the United States to import $80 million of coal in exchange for steel exports of the same value.
Deputy Industry Minister Marin Marinov said Kremikovtzi's prices were competitive especially for semi-finished steel, assisted by lower labour costs and less stringent environmental regulations.
"Here in the East you are much more competitive because you have lower labour costs," he said.
Milushev said the plant was investing to keep in line with Bulgaria's environmental regulations but declined to comment on how the plant compared with enterprises in Western Europe.

Previous governments dragged their feet on reforms already far advanced in other East European countries but quick action has been forced on Bulgaria by the virtual collapse of the economy late last year and the imposition of a currency board regime, whose restrictions include a ban on government subsidies to state enterprises.
